note: To drag someone down with your own troubles. You feel the guilt in it: 不想拖累你 is what you say when your illness or debt could sink someone you love.
To hold back money that's owed, especially wages. You hear 拖欠工资 and picture migrant workers waiting for their pay as Spring Festival gets closer.
To hem and haw so you don't have to answer. You can hear it in 支支吾吾: the mumbling, the half sentences, the look away.
The thin, sharp chill of early spring. It's a bookish word, and in 春寒料峭 you feel a cold wind at your neck while the sun is already out.
To get at something indirectly, through hints. You picture tapping at the side instead of knocking on the front: you ask about something nearby and watch how they react.
Rather too much, said as a mild criticism. When you say 未免太贵了, you're objecting while keeping it polite, like clearing your throat.
To weigh the pros and cons. You picture an old steelyard scale, its 权 and 衡, with each side held up in your hand before you decide.
The documents an office wants from you. When you're told to 准备材料, you picture a stack of ID copies, certificates and stamped forms, and probably a second trip.
Someone cut out for something. You say 我不是学习的材料 with a shrug, as if you were simply the wrong stuff for it.
Furious and flustered, with your composure gone. You picture someone red-faced and scrambling because things have gone against them, and it's a little satisfying to watch.
Properly run and above board, not fly-by-night. When you call a company 正规, you're reassured: there's a contract, your insurance gets paid and your wages arrive on time.
To obey what comes from above. You may remember ticking 服从调剂 on a university form, agreeing to go wherever you were put.
